_meta: Two transactions that each need the same two resources in opposite order, and a retry policy, used to show livelock -- a failure where processes keep changing state in response to each other and make no progress, even though none is blocked -- and why the fix is to break the symmetry of their retries. Transaction 0 wants resource A then B; transaction 1 wants B then A. Each round both grab their first resource (they differ, so both succeed), then each fails to get its second (the other holds it), so each politely releases what it holds and retries. This is not deadlock: in deadlock each would hold its first resource and wait forever, a cycle a detector can find and break; here the resources are released every round, so a deadlock detector finds nothing to abort -- the system is fully active, just accomplishing nothing. If both retry on the same schedule (lockstep), the next round is identical to the last, and they repeat forever, zero transactions completing. The cure is to make their retries asymmetric so the tie is broken: on a conflict, back off by an amount that differs between the two (here, by transaction id), so one retries while the other is still waiting, gets both resources, completes, and frees the way for the other. Randomized backoff achieves the same by making a repeat of the exact schedule vanishingly unlikely. resource_order maps each transaction to the order it acquires the two resources; max_rounds bounds the simulation; asymmetric_backoff is the per-transaction extra wait used by the fix. These are the fixture; the completions and per-round state under lockstep and under asymmetric retry are computed.
